h.strategy: Read the retrieved abstracts for measured results that contradict common heuristics: options that were expected to be weak but did well, gains that vanished in strong configurations, or components whose value depended on what else was present. Turn each such finding into a conditional claim about when a one-field edit's effect is larger or smaller. Each hypothesis must cite the kind of evidence it rests on in one sentence. Avoid hypotheses that only restate that removing an alternative path makes the remaining path matter more. Vary the edited and conditioning fields, and balance HIGHER and LOWER.

hyps.why: Reported NAS-Bench-201 results show diminishing returns from extra 3x3 convs once a strong direct conv path to the output already exists.
Replacing a removed edge with a 3x3 conv adds capacity and gives a larger gain than swapping out an already-parametric or skip op.
Skip connections on the direct input-output edge are known to be surprisingly strong, so replacing one with a conv yields little or negative gain.
Stacked parameter-free pooling blurs features and was observed to hurt, so adding pooling after pooling is worse than adding it elsewhere.
Edge 2 is dead when node 1 has no input, so removing it costs far less than when it carries real signal.
Skip connections help most when they pass forward learned conv features, a pattern seen with residual-style gains that depend on the paths around them.
Gains from an additional conv branch vanish when a strong conv path is already present, as seen in saturating strong configurations.
A cheap 1x1 conv on an internal edge pairs well with a downstream 3x3 conv, so a component's value depends on its neighbors.
Redundant skip connections add little, so a second skip into the output gains less than the first.
Deep conv chains (0->1->2->3) increase receptive field and depth, so the first conv edge in the chain matters more when its successor is also a conv.
